DecSummary: The worker suffered a shoulder injury when he slipped and fell in February 2013. The employer terminated the worker's employer in June 2013. The Panel agreed with the approach in Decisions No. 904/14 and 2816/18, that it is not sufficient to determinate that the termination was not injury-related; rather, it must be demonstrated that the worker's conduct was such that the worker should be he responsible for the loss of employment and associated wages. In this case, the worker violated the employer's strict ant-harassment and anti-discrimination policy in April 2013 and in June 2013. In April, he was given the opportunity to cease his conduct that violated the policy and he was warned that any future violation would result in termination of his employment. The worker was not entitled to LOE benefits following the termination of his employment, except for a period in September 2013, when he was recovering from compensable shoulder surgery.

DecSummary: The worker's application for reconsideration of Decision No. 2751/18 was granted. DecSummary: The worker was entitled to full LOE benefits for the period in question from September 2012 to November 2013. Simply identifying a number of NOC-coded occupations as requiring no training and as being potentially suitable for a worker does not constitute a determination through the WT process that any one or all of such jobs would be achievable for the worker without training. The WT process requires a collaborative effort in determining an appropriate SO. In this case, the worker, his representative and the WT specialist ultimately determined an appropriate entry level SO, listed in the NOC codes as requiring no training, but through the collaborative effort identified the need for eight weeks of academic upgrading, five weeks of college level training, two weeks of job search training and 10 weeks of training on the job. The worker was entitled to full LOE benefits for the prior period.

The worker's application for reconsideration of Decision No. 1419/18 was denied. The worker submitted that the hearing panel erred by limiting the weight given to a medical report which was filed without the letter from the representative soliciting the report. However, the Vice-Chair noted that the Tribunal practice direction on Expert Evidence makes clear that a party filing a medical report is required to provide the letter asking for the report. Representatives appearing at the Tribunal are expected to be familiar with the Tribunal's practice directions. The obligation is on the representative to file the report in accordance with the practice direction. The failure to do so ran the risk that the hearing panel would limit the weight given to the report.

DecSummary: Decision No. 3370/18 found that the worker did not have a permanent impairment. The worker applied for reconsideration of Decision No. 3370/18. The original vice-chair appeared to rely on a comment in a letter from the worker indicating that he was feeling 100% after surgery. In Decision No. 3370/18R, the Vice-Chair noted that an impairment is defined as a physical or functional abnormality or loss. Feeling 100% is not the same as not having an impairment. It appears that the original vice-chair failed to consider the statutory definition of impairment and permanent impairment. In Decision No. 3370/18R, the Vice-Chair found that the worker has made an arguable case that Decision No. 3370/18 contained a significant error. Accordingly, the Vice-Chair directed that the employer be provided with an opportunity to make submissions on the threshold test for reconsideration.

DecSummary: The worker suffered a shoulder injury in December 2013. The Panel found that the worker was entitled to LOE benefits from November 2014 to December 2014, while attending a Board pain program. The Board denied benefits on the basis that the worker was not working at the time of the program because she had refused suitable work offered by the employer. The Panel found that it was not necessary to determine whether the worker refused suitable work. By attending the program, the worker was co-operating in health care measures. The WSIA and Board policy provide that benefits may be reduced or suspended if a worker is not co-operating in ESRTW or health care measures; it follows that, absent such non-co-operation, it is expected that an eligible worker will continue to receive benefits. DecSummary: Decision No. 121/18 denied the worker entitlement for a recurrence in 2009 of a low back injury suffered in 1994. The worker's application for reconsideration of Decision No. 121/18 was denied. There was no error in the original decision when the vice-chair considered the effects of a pre-existing non-compensable low back condition for which the worker had undergone surgery. The fact that the NEL award for the compensable injury was not reduced due to the pre-existing condition, did not have the effect of binding the vice-chair on the appeal to a determination that the worker did not have a pre-existing condition, nor did it prohibit the vice-chair from considering whether that condition progressed in the years following the accident. The Vice-Chair also noted that the Board decision not to reduce a NEL award on account of a pre-existing impairment did not mean that the Board turned its attention to whether the worker had a pre-existing condition at the time of the workplace accident.

The Board recalculated the worker's long-term earnings basis. The Vice-Chair found that the short length of employment with the accident employer was not a basis upon which to recalculate the worker's long-term earnings. DecSummary: Rather than a significant deterioration in the chronic upper extremity condition, the real change in this case was the employer's decision to discontinue the worker's employment beyond November 2011. The Panel notes that section 44(2.1)(g) of the WSIA permits additional review of FEL benefits if, as in this case, the worker and the employer were cooperating in return to work at the 60-month point. Unfortunately for the worker, however, such further review is allowed for two additional years only (in this case, to 2000). There is no separate exception authorizing post-60-month FEL review when an employer withdraws modified work, and none of the other exceptions within section 44(2.1) of the WSIA apply to the facts of this appeal. Consequently, pursuant to section 44(2) of the WSIA, there is no authority for the worker's FEL benefit to be adjusted in 2011 as requested.

DecKeywords: Carpal tunnel syndrome; Disablement (nature of work)
DecSummary: The worker did not have entitlement for carpal tunnel syndrome. The worker's condition was not a disablement from the nature of his work. Carpal tunnel syndrome is a common medical condition with many potential causes. For carpal tunnel syndrome to be related to workplace duties, those duties must be repetitive and strenuous, and there should be a temporal relationship to the development of symptoms. In this case, the worker's duties sometimes involved strenuous use of the hands but were repetitive for only limited periods of time. Tasks were well varied, and strenuous use of the hands was not continuous. There was no temporal relationship established between the onset of symptoms and the job duties performed.

DecSummary: Decision 2034/18R granted the employer's request for reconsideration. In accordance with that decision, the Vice-Chair reheard the worker's appeal. The appeal was allowed and the worker granted entitlement for a L4-5 disc herniation for a September 2014 accident. The medical evidence supported a finding that the accident was a significant contributing factor to the disc herniation.

The worker had entitlement for lung cancer as a result of exposure to asbestos and silica while working in construction. The Tribunal's Medical Assessor concluded that the worker was exposed to moderate levels of asbestos based on the existence of pleural plaques, and also had exposure to silica. Given the worker's minimal smoking history, the Medical Assessor attributed his cancer to the occupational exposures. The Medical Assessor's opinion was the most reliable medical evidence available and was consistent with an earlier medical opinion attributing the worker's cancer to his workplace exposures.

DecKeywords: Suitable employment; Loss of earnings {LOE}; Psychotraumatic disability; Recurrences (compensable injury); Board Directives and Guidelines (LOE) (lay-off)
DecSummary: The worker, an electrician/foreman, sustained a low back injury in January 2011 for which he received a 9% NEL award. The worker was diagnosed with major depressive disorder (MDD) in 2012 and granted entitlement for psychotraumatic disability on a temporary basis. The worker returned to work with the accident employer in the SO of construction estimator/project manager. He was off work from December 17, 2014 to January 5, 2015 because the employer said it did not have work for him. He returned to work on January 5, 2015 in a job fabricating aluminum cable trays, but stopped working on January 26, 2015 and claimed a recurrence of psychotraumatic disability.  The worker appealed a decision of the Appeals Resolution Officer denying entitlement to LOE benefits from December 17, 2014 to January 5, 2015 as a result of a temporary layoff, determining that the aluminum tray assembly job was suitable, and denying entitlement to an aggravation of his psychological condition and LOE benefits from January 26, 2015.

DecKeywords: Consequences of injury; Delay (onset of symptoms); Permanent impairment {NEL}; Loss of earnings {LOE} (termination of employment)
DecSummary: The worker, a bookkeeper, was injured in February 2008 while standing on a step ladder to put a box on a shelf above her head. She was granted entitlement for thoracic and cervical spine strains, and received a NEL award for her thoracic spine. She attempted to a gradual return with the accident employer, but left in August 2008. She began self-employment in March 2009. Her appeal of an Appeals Resolution Officer decision denying entitlement for a permanent neck impairment, ischemic colitis, vertigo, left ulnar neuritis, and LOE benefits after August 2008 was dismissed in Decision No. 740/18. Decision No. 740/18R granted the worker's request for reconsideration.

The worker's application for reconsideration of Decision No. 1266/18 was dismissed. The worker was attempting to reargue the appeal. The worker's submissions in support of the reconsideration request were all matters that were argued before the panel in the appeal. None of the information presented suggested there was an error with the decision that if corrected, would lead to a different result. The decision was reasonable and supported by the totality of the evidence.

The worker's representative sought an adjournment. The Panel found that the primary argument being advanced by the worker's representative, that CPD applied to both claims, was not jurisdictionally before the Tribunal as there was no 'final decision' of the Board within the meaning of subsection 123(1) of the WSIA.
